passage: I'm Dolma, and for the clean-lake week I wrote a slogan on chart paper: 'Our lake, our shame, fix it now.' I was proud of it, short and loud. Then my friend Anirban read it and frowned. "Shame? It sounds like you're blaming the whole colony, including the old aunties who've swept that shore for years." I hadn't meant that at all. I meant urgency. I looked at it again and saw that a short line can lean in several directions at once. I tried three more until I found 'Our lake, our care, start today.' My caption for the photo went with it, and it felt warmer. I'm still learning that fewer words means each one carries more.

qa.q: What was Dolma's first slogan?
qa.a: Dolma's first slogan was 'Our lake, our shame, fix it now.'

qa.q: Why did Anirban frown at the word shame?
qa.a: Anirban felt it sounded like blaming the whole colony, including the older neighbours who had cleaned the shore for years. Dolma had meant urgency, so the same words carried a different message for Anirban.

qa.q: What could Dolma try when writing a slogan next time?
qa.a: Show it to a few different people first and ask how each one reads it, then adjust the words.

qa.q: How might one of the aunties who sweep the shore feel about the first slogan?
qa.a: They might feel accused or overlooked, despite their years of work.

grounding: A teen writes a slogan and learns short forms compress attitude and can be read differently by different audiences.

passage: Note, Friday. The Class Nine skit script by Kashish arrived on my desk with the line, 'Everyone in this town is afraid of the truth.' She had also written a caption for the poster: 'Speak up, or stay silent forever.' The words are strong, and I can see she cares about speaking up. But I asked her to imagine how a shy student, or a parent in the audience, might hear them. She was quiet for a bit, then said she hadn't thought of that and wondered if the line sounded like a scolding. She's going to try 'Some of us are afraid of the truth, and that's human.' I will help with the caption too. Avni, drama teacher.

qa.q: What did the poster caption say?
qa.a: The caption said, 'Speak up, or stay silent forever.'

qa.q: What might Kashish have felt when asked how a shy student would hear the line?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised and a bit self-conscious, since she says she hadn't thought of it and wonders if it sounds like scolding. She clearly cares about the message.

qa.q: What could Kashish do with the caption?
qa.a: Try softer, more inclusive wording and test it on a few readers.

qa.q: How might a shy student in the audience feel about the original line?
qa.a: They may feel accused or pressured, instead of invited.

grounding: A teen's script and caption compress attitude, and different audiences read them differently.

passage:
Tuesday, late. Salma's diary.

I messed up with Elizabeth today. She sent me a photo of her science project and I typed, "wow nice job genius" meaning it as a joke because we tease each other. No emoji, because my thumb slipped. She didn't answer for an hour. Then she wrote, "ok." That's all. I thought, oh no. Did she read it as sarcasm? I could imagine it two ways: me being nice, or me being mean.

So I called her. It took six rings. "I meant it kindly," I said. She laughed, relieved. "I thought you thought it was bad." I'll add a smiley next time. Or just call. 🙂

qa.q: What did Salma type about Elizabeth's science project?
qa.a: Salma typed, "wow nice job genius".

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth answer only "ok"?
qa.a: She may have read the message as sarcastic and felt hurt or unsure, since there was no smiley and no voice to show the tone. Salma guessed this and called.

qa.q: What could Salma do in future to avoid this?
qa.a: Add a smiley or a clarifying line, or call when the tone might be unclear.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt during the hour of silence?
qa.a: She was probably worried or upset, thinking Salma thought her project was bad.

grounding: A joking message reads as rude because face and voice are missing, and a call clears it up.

passage:
Yash: i can't come to your birthday
Rashmi: haha nice one 😅
Yash: no seriously. i have to go to my grandma's, she isn't well
Rashmi: oh no. wait i thought you were joking
Yash: i wasn't. sorry i should have said it more clearly
Rashmi: no it's my fault, i laughed. i'm sorry about your grandma
Yash: thanks. i really wanted to come
Rashmi: can we do a small cake at your place on sunday?
Yash: yes please 🙂
Rashmi: i'll bring it after class. and message me if you want to talk

qa.q: Why can't Yash come to Rashmi's birthday?
qa.a: Yash has to visit a grandma who isn't well.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi laugh at Yash's first message?
qa.a: Rashmi thought Yash was joking, because a message like that can look like teasing when nobody can see a face or hear a voice. Rashmi then felt bad once the truth was clear.

qa.q: What could either of them do next time to avoid the mix-up?
qa.a: Yash could add a line like 'no seriously' early, and Rashmi could check with a question before reacting.

qa.q: How might Yash have felt on seeing the laughing reaction?
qa.a: Yash may have felt hurt or misunderstood at a worrying time. 🤍

grounding: A serious message read as a joke because face and voice are missing, and a clarifying line resolves it.

passage: Vinita, in my day we had no hearts or thumbs, and somehow we worried just the same. When I was seventeen I once wrote a long letter to a friend, and she didn't reply for three weeks. I decided she didn't like me. Then I found out her family had moved cities. You have those little reaction buttons now, and I've seen you go quiet when a friend didn't tap one on your post. Remember my letter. A thumbs-up is a quick way to say 'I saw you, well done', and it costs nothing to give. But when it doesn't come, it usually means she was busy, or asleep, or the phone was off. Ask her at lunch. Rafiq, your grandfather.

qa.q: How long did the friend not reply to Rafiq's letter?
qa.a: She did not reply for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq decide the friend didn't like him?
qa.a: He felt hurt by the silence and assumed the worst, before learning that her family had moved cities. His story shows how easily a missing signal is over-read.

qa.q: What advice does Rafiq give Vinita when a friend does not react to Vinita's post?
qa.a: Do not read it as rejection, and simply ask the friend in person.

qa.q: How might Vinita's friend feel if Vinita went quiet over a missing thumbs-up?
qa.a: She might be surprised and upset, since she may not even have noticed the post.

grounding: An elder says reaction buttons are lightweight signals, and a missing reaction should not be over-read.

passage: It was the night before exams, the power kept flickering, and Parul's phone had one bar of signal. She posted a photo of her notes with the caption 'wish me luck', then tapped a heart on Harish's post about his last revision session. Harish, at his desk with a candle beside him, saw her heart and felt lighter. She waited. Nobody reacted to hers for an hour. Her stomach dropped. Then she remembered what her grandfather had said and told herself: the network is bad and everybody is studying. She switched it off and went back to the chapter. In the morning, Harish sent, 'Good luck! I saw your post late, network was down.' She smiled and put her pen in her bag.

qa.q: What did Parul tap on Harish's post?
qa.a: She tapped a heart.

qa.q: Why did Parul's stomach drop when nobody reacted?
qa.a: She felt worried that people didn't care or that she was not supported, at a stressful time. Then she reminded herself that the network and studying could explain it.

qa.q: What did Parul do that helped her cope?
qa.a: She reminded herself of a likelier explanation and put the phone away to study.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt when he saw Parul's heart?
qa.a: He felt lighter, since the heart was a quick sign of support during a tense night.

grounding: Reaction buttons are lightweight signals, and a missing reaction should not be over-read.

subtype: Memes and GIFs as shared language [Expressing]
passage:
Dear Leela,

You asked why I laughed so hard in the class chat last night. Someone posted a GIF of a cat pushing a glass off a table, and I replied with another of a cat looking guilty, because of what happened to Ms Rao's vase last term. Only about seven of us know why that's funny. Then a new boy, Kabir, wrote, 'I don't get it, is this about me?' I realised our in-joke had made him feel outside. So I explained the story and he laughed too. It shows how a picture can carry so much for some people and nothing for others.

Best,
Chetan 🙂

qa.q: Whose vase does the guilty-cat GIF refer to?
qa.a: It refers to Ms Rao's vase from last term.

qa.q: Why did Kabir write, 'I don't get it, is this about me?'
qa.a: He felt left out and worried the joke was aimed at him, since he did not know the story behind it. He said so openly, which is a good sign.

qa.q: What could Chetan do next time before posting an in-joke?
qa.a: Add a short line that explains the story or send it only to the friends who know it.

qa.q: How might the seven who know the joke see it?
qa.a: As a warm shared laugh, without noticing that it could shut others out.

grounding: A teen replies with a GIF to convey humour and belonging, and an in-joke may confuse outsiders.

subtype: Memes and GIFs as shared language [Expressing]
passage: Afreen, you asked how the meme thing went wrong. So we have this group where we send a picture of a tired panda every time someone fails a test. It means 'I feel you, I've been there'. Last week Ranjan, a new kid, failed a maths quiz, and someone sent the panda. He wrote back, 'Are you saying I'm lazy?' And I realised: he doesn't know it means we're with him. For us, it's a hug. For him, it looked like teasing. I sent him a private message, 'That panda is our way of saying we've all failed too.' He replied with a thumbs-up. Next time I'll explain a joke before I use it. Zubin, over and out.

qa.q: What picture does the group send when someone fails a test?
qa.a: They send a picture of a tired panda.

qa.q: Why did Ranjan ask whether he was being called lazy?
qa.a: He did not know the panda was a friendly sign, so he read it as teasing about his failure and probably felt hurt or embarrassed.

qa.q: What did Zubin do that helped?
qa.a: Zubin sent Ranjan a private message explaining that the panda means everyone has failed too.

qa.q: How might the friends who sent the panda have felt about Ranjan's reply?
qa.a: They may have been surprised, since they meant it kindly.

grounding: A teen uses a meme to convey belonging, and an in-joke may hurt outsiders.

passage: Before posting the photo from Saturday's trek, I tried three filters. I made the sky bluer and cropped out the muddy trousers. I wrote the caption 'Living my best life.' That was true, but it wasn't the whole truth, because I'd also slipped twice and been grumpy for an hour, and nobody would see it. I said this to Sudha, who laughed and said, "Everyone's feed is curated, Mohit. That's why mine looks calm too." I thought about that and posted it. But I asked Sudha before I put up the group shot she was in. She said yes to that one and no to the one where she was blinking. Now I try to remember that a post is a selected slice.

qa.q: How many filters did Mohit try on the trek photo?
qa.a: Mohit tried three filters.

qa.q: Why did Mohit feel that the caption was true but not the whole truth?
qa.a: Mohit felt the caption showed only the happy part and hid the two slips and the grumpy hour. Mohit realised what people see is chosen.

qa.q: What did Mohit do that showed care for a friend's image?
qa.a: Mohit asked Sudha before posting the group photo and accepted her no to the picture where she was blinking.

qa.q: How might a viewer who sees only the post feel about their own life?
qa.a: They might feel their day is duller or harder than others', not knowing it is curated.

grounding: A teen curates photos and captions for self-presentation, knows posts are a slice, and shares others' images with consent.

passage: Counselling note, Monday. Raghav came in after a classmate told him off for posting a class photo in which she was making a funny face. Raghav said she'd laughed at the time, so he thought it was fine. She hadn't said yes, and she has now asked him to remove it. He also mentioned that his own feed looks like everyone has amazing weekends, and that he sometimes feels bad comparing. We talked about how people choose the best photos and filters, and how other people's pictures need their permission. He agreed to take the photo down and ask before posting in future. I told him he can talk to me any time. Vidya, counsellor.

qa.q: What did Raghav's friend tell him off for?
qa.a: She told him off for posting a class photo in which she was making a funny face.

qa.q: What was Raghav thinking when he posted the photo?
qa.a: He believed that because she had laughed, it was fine. He had not asked her, so he had not checked what she felt.

qa.q: What steps did Raghav agree to?
qa.a: Take the photo down and ask before posting anyone's image in future.

qa.q: How might Raghav's friend have felt seeing the photo online?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed and exposed, since the picture went out without her say.

grounding: A teen curates a self-image and learns personal images should be shared only with consent.

passage: Kunal's phone lit up: 'okay.' Just that, lowercase, with a full stop. He stared at it. Samir was usually all capital letters and exclamation marks. A full stop felt like a closed door. Kunal wrote back, 'you good?' Two minutes later, 'OKAY!!! sorry, was in the middle of football and my hands were muddy.' Kunal grinned and typed, 'sooooo you're not angry?' Samir sent, 'Lol no, I was just typing with one thumb.' Kunal put the phone away, half laughing at himself. On the walk to school he said, "Your full stops are scary, you know." Samir shrugged. "They're just how I type when I'm rushed." They agreed to ask when in doubt.

qa.q: What was Samir's first message?
qa.a: It was 'okay.' in lowercase with a full stop.

qa.q: Why did Kunal write 'you good?' after the first message?
qa.a: The lowercase word with a full stop felt cold to him, and he worried Samir might be upset. He could not tell the mood without checking.

qa.q: What could Kunal do when a short message feels cold?
qa.a: Ask a light question like 'you good?', because punctuation suggests a mood but does not prove it.

qa.q: How might Samir have seen Samir's own message?
qa.a: As an ordinary quick reply typed with one thumb, with no cold meaning. 🙂

grounding: Punctuation and capitalisation are read for mood in text, but they suggest and do not prove.

passage:
"Look at this," said Swati, holding out her phone. "She wrote 'fine.' Full stop. She never uses full stops."
"So?" said Yogesh.
"So she's angry."
"Or she's busy. Or her keyboard's odd." He scrolled up. "Here she wrote 'sooooo excited!!!' last night. That's her being playful, not her being loud."
"It's just confusing. Some of my friends use capitals to shout and some to be happy."
"Then you can't tell from the letters," said Yogesh. "You'd have to ask."
Swati sighed and typed, 'you okay? your fine sounded serious.' The reply came fast: 'haha sorry, I was in the middle of a test. I'm fine!'

qa.q: What did Swati's friend write?
qa.a: She wrote 'fine.' with a full stop.

qa.q: Why did Swati think her friend was angry?
qa.a: She noticed the full stop, which the friend never used, and read it as a sign of cold or angry mood. Yogesh pointed out other explanations such as being busy or a keyboard quirk.

qa.q: What could Swati try instead of guessing?
qa.a: Ask the friend directly if she is okay, as she did.

qa.q: How might the friend feel when she reads Swati's question?
qa.a: She may feel cared for and amused, since she was just in the middle of a test.

grounding: Punctuation and capitalisation suggest a mood but do not prove it, and asking is wiser.

subtype: Drama and mime as emotional language [Expressing]
passage: Drama teacher's note, Thursday. In improvisation class I gave everyone the prompt 'a goodbye'. Lalremsiami, without words, performed a mime of someone holding an empty coat and standing at a door for a long time. The room was completely still. Afterwards some students wiped their eyes. I did not ask whether it was about her own life. I said only, "That was powerful. How did the role feel to play?" She said, "Heavy, but it felt good to let it out somewhere." I noticed she was not distressed. Acting lets a person explore an emotion at a distance, and does not tell us her own story. I will check in privately next week anyway. Damini.

qa.q: What was the improvisation prompt?
qa.a: The prompt was 'a goodbye'.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami seem to feel after the mime?
qa.a: She said the role felt heavy but good to let out, and she did not seem distressed. The stillness in the room suggests the mime moved her audience.

qa.q: Why did Damini not ask whether the mime was about Lalremsiami's own life?
qa.a: Because role work is a safe way to explore feelings and does not mean the performer is telling her own story. Damini still chose a private check-in in case Lalremsiami wanted to talk.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami's classmates have felt watching the mime?
qa.a: Many felt moved, since some wiped their eyes.

grounding: A teen uses mime to portray grief at a safe distance, and role work is not a confession.

subtype: Drama and mime as emotional language [Expressing]
passage:
Friday, 8 pm.

Today in drama, Ms Iyer told us to improvise being furious. I didn't want to, but Keerthana whispered, "Just try it." So I became a character whose lunch had been stolen for the tenth time, and I shouted, stomped and threw my script on the floor. My voice shook a bit. Everyone clapped. Afterwards my chest felt loose, like a fist had opened. Ayesha, that's me, I have a lot of anger about the group project and I never say it. I didn't say it today either, but the role let me feel it safely.

Ms Iyer asked, "Was that about something real?" I said, "A bit. But mostly it was a character." She nodded and didn't push. 😊

qa.q: What did the character in Ayesha's improvisation lose?
qa.a: The character's lunch had been stolen for the tenth time.

qa.q: What did Ayesha feel after the improvisation?
qa.a: Ayesha's chest felt loose, like a fist had opened, so some tension eased. Ayesha also admits to real anger about the group project that stays unsaid.

qa.q: What could Ayesha try next if the anger about the project stays?
qa.a: Tell a trusted person or the group calmly about it, since acting only lets Ayesha feel it safely.

qa.q: How might Ms Iyer have felt when Ayesha said it was a bit real?
qa.a: She may have felt attentive and careful, and chose not to push while keeping the door open.

grounding: A teen improvises anger through drama, and role work explores emotion safely but is not a confession.

subtype: Playlists and dance trends as mood signals [Mismatch]
passage: Aparna's story on the video site showed a slow, sad song with a grey picture of rain, captioned, "Mood." Akash saw it while eating breakfast and frowned. Aparna usually posted memes. Was she sad? Or was it a trend? He remembered that last week half the class had posted the same song for a dance challenge. He didn't reply with 'are you okay??' in front of everyone. Instead he sent her a private message, 'Hey, nice song. How's your day going?' Aparna wrote back, 'Honestly it's a dance routine for the fest, we picked the saddest song!! But thanks for asking 🙂'. Akash laughed with relief, and told her he'd come to the practice.

qa.q: What word did Aparna use to caption her story?
qa.a: She captioned her story, "Mood."

qa.q: What was Akash wondering when he saw the sad song?
qa.a: He wondered whether Aparna was sad or just following a trend, since she usually posted memes. He decided not to assume.

qa.q: What made Akash's approach kind and useful?
qa.a: He sent a private, friendly message to check in, without alarming her in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Aparna have felt if Akash had publicly asked 'are you okay??'
qa.a: She might have felt embarrassed or surprised, since it was just a dance routine.

grounding: A teen's sad song can mean mood, humour, belonging or fashion, and a brief kind check-in is better than assuming distress.

subtype: Playlists and dance trends as mood signals [Mismatch]
passage:
"Have you seen Mridul's post?" Eshaan asked. "The song is so sad."
"He's doing that dance thing everyone's doing," said his sister.
"But he added a caption. 'Can't shake this one.'"
"That might mean he's stuck on the tune. Or that he's feeling low. I can't tell."
"Should I say something?"
"Just a quick message. Nothing dramatic."
Eshaan wrote to Mridul: 'Love the song. Everything okay with you or is it just the dance craze?'
Mridul answered within minutes: 'Ha, dance craze, and also I failed a quiz and the song fits. But I'm fine. Thanks for checking.'
Eshaan sent back a hug. "Good," said his sister. "That was the right size of check-in."

qa.q: What did Mridul's caption say?
qa.a: His caption said, 'Can't shake this one.'

qa.q: What might Mridul's post have meant, according to Eshaan's sister?
qa.a: It might mean he is stuck on the tune or that he is feeling low, and she cannot tell. Mridul later says it was the dance craze and a failed quiz.

qa.q: What made Eshaan's check-in the right size?
qa.a: It was short, private and friendly, and asked whether it was something serious or just a trend without assuming anything.

qa.q: How might Mridul have felt when Eshaan checked in?
qa.a: He probably felt noticed and cared for, since he answered quickly and thanked him.

grounding: A sad song or dance trend can mean mood or fashion, and a brief check-in beats assuming distress.

passage: I write verses in the notebook under my bed. One I wrote in Class Eleven began, 'I'm a storm in a jar, and the jar is breaking.' I was angry about a fight with my parents, so I exaggerated it. When I read it aloud at the school slam poetry evening, some people in the audience stared, and one teacher, Mr Kamal, came up afterwards and asked quietly, "That was strong. Is that how you feel, or is it a character?" I said, "A bit of both. The storm is real, but I'm not going to break anything." He nodded. I liked that he asked instead of guessing. Poems let me shout on paper. Arohi.

qa.q: Where did Arohi read the verse aloud?
qa.a: Arohi read it at the school slam poetry evening.

qa.q: What did Mr Kamal want to know when he asked if it was a character?
qa.a: He wanted to understand whether the words described Arohi's real feelings or plans, or were a persona. He asked calmly instead of assuming.

qa.q: What would you advise a listener who hears a very dark lyric?
qa.a: Ask the writer kindly what it means, and take any talk of real harm seriously by getting help from a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might the audience members who stared have felt?
qa.a: Some may have been unsettled or moved, not knowing whether the words were real.

grounding: A teen writes verses using persona and exaggeration, and a listener asks the writer before assuming.

passage: Teacher's note, Monday. Kunal handed in the rap he'd written for the talent show. One verse said, 'I'll burn this whole town down, they never see me.' I felt uneasy and my first thought was to call his parents. Then I remembered that lyrics use exaggeration and persona, so I invited Bhavna, our counsellor, and Kunal to talk. Kunal explained, a little embarrassed, that the verse was about feeling invisible after his friends moved to another school, not about hurting anyone. He agreed to change the line, though he wanted to keep the 'invisible' image. Bhavna will check on how he's feeling about the friends. Class teacher.

qa.q: What did Kunal's verse say about the town?
qa.a: It said, 'I'll burn this whole town down, they never see me.'

qa.q: What was Kunal really feeling behind the line about the town?
qa.a: He was feeling invisible after his friends moved to another school, and the line was an exaggeration, not a plan. He was also a little embarrassed about being asked.

qa.q: What could Bhavna do next?
qa.a: Check on how he is coping with the lost friendships, and keep an open door for him to talk.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt when he was called in?
qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed or worried he was in trouble, yet relieved that the adults asked instead of assuming.

grounding: A teen writes lyrics with exaggeration, and a caring adult asks the writer what the words mean.

passage: My little sister Shreya has a habit that used to worry me. After an argument, she goes to her room and draws for an hour, not talking. Last week she and Papa had a big fight about her marks. Her face was red. She went to the room and I heard her pencil scratching. I peeked in and saw a drawing of a boat in a storm, and a small lantern glowing in the boat's corner. When she came out, her face had gone from red to calm. I can't say what she felt exactly, maybe relieved, maybe tired. But I noticed she talked to Papa gently at dinner. Drawing seems to lower her intensity, and if I ever see her only drawing dark things and not eating, I'll tell Mama. Manjula.

qa.q: What did Shreya draw after the fight with Papa?
qa.a: She drew a boat in a storm with a small lantern glowing in a corner.

qa.q: What might Shreya's drawing and calm face suggest?
qa.a: They suggest the drawing helped her work through her anger and tension. Manjula admits being unable to know exactly what Shreya felt.

qa.q: What would signal that Manjula should talk to a trusted adult?
qa.a: If Shreya only drew dark things and withdrew, for example not eating, Manjula would tell their mother.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Shreya spoke gently at dinner?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved and softened toward her.

grounding: Art works as a private outlet for stress, and persistent dark themes with withdrawal would call for a caring conversation.

passage:
Monday. Tejas started editing a video on his phone after his parents argued. The clips were slow and grey, and the music was low. Hrithik, his older cousin, glanced at it and said nothing. Tejas seemed calmer afterwards.
Wednesday. The videos got darker, and Tejas stopped coming to cricket and barely spoke at dinner. He told Hrithik, "I'm fine, it's just art."
Friday. Hrithik sat beside him. "Your videos help you, I can tell. But you've gone quiet lately. Not judging, just asking. What's going on?" Tejas exhaled. "I don't know. I feel heavy." Hrithik said, "Let's tell Auntie together. She'll listen." Tejas nodded and handed him the phone.

qa.q: What did Tejas start editing on Monday?
qa.a: He started editing a video on his phone.

qa.q: Why did Tejas say 'I'm fine, it's just art' on Wednesday?
qa.a: He may have wanted to avoid worrying anyone, or he was not ready to say how heavy he felt. The darker videos and his withdrawal showed there was more to it.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do that helped?
qa.a: Hrithik said the question was not judgement, named what he noticed and offered to go to Tejas's mother together.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when Hrithik asked him directly?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved that someone noticed, and also a bit nervous.

grounding: Art helps a teen through stress, and persistent dark themes with withdrawal call for a caring conversation, not judgement.
